Knorvia-authored provenance similarity tooling. The dual-comparison wrapper now measures the upstream side even for candidates that are unchanged from the baseline. Those candidates always score one against their own old version, but the upstream figure is still the only evidence for telling an inherited file apart from one that was rewritten, so reporting it keeps a whole class of files diagnosable. Both upstream-only invocations now declare allow-upstream-only explicitly, since the gate rejects a missing old file by design, and the unchanged branch prints the upstream containment and longest run alongside the unchanged verdict. Verified with the wrapper guard tests and by re-running an unchanged candidate, which reports upstream containment one point zero and a run of twenty-one.

Knorvia-authored provenance similarity tooling. The gate now refuses to degrade silently to an upstream-only comparison. The plan requires the two thresholds to pass against both the replaced old file and the fixed upstream commit, but the old-file side could previously vanish without a word: paths that did not resolve at the given revision were filtered out of the comparison set, and omitting the old file altogether was syntactically valid. Both situations now exit with an error that names the missing paths and explains why the silent fallback was rejected. A genuine upstream-only measurement remains possible by passing allow-upstream-only explicitly, in which case the run prints a note that the result is not a completion basis under the plan. The dual-comparison wrapper accepts that flag through to the tool, and a candidate whose worktree content equals the baseline revision is reported as unchanged-from-baseline and judged failing, because an unmodified file is by definition identical to its old version. Verified with sixty tests, including four new cases for a missing old path, an omitted old path, an explicit upstream-only run, and a normal dual comparison.

New Knorvia regression tests for the declaration-mode purity guard: a named const block is only exempt from scoring when it is pure data (literal arrays/objects, z.enum, Object.freeze), while functions, conditions, arithmetic, spreads, interpolated templates and computed calls keep their lines scored. Node built-ins only; no upstream test was copied or adapted. License follows licensing/README.md for new scripts/provenance tools.

Knorvia-authored provenance similarity tooling. The gate now prints the residual and removed contract lines verbatim, because the acceptance documents require quoting the remaining code rather than only reporting how many lines were removed. The residual output lists the kept lines with their one-based numbers in the original text, and the removed output does the same for the lines that were excluded, so a reviewer can both verify that the remaining part is what still needs rework and check that exclusion did not reach too far. A configurable limit defaults to fifty lines per section and reports the total when truncated. The removed-line records carry source line numbers now that they are surfaced, and the exclusion counter is derived from the same loop so the two cannot drift apart. Verified with sixty-four tests, including residual-and-removed dumping and the line-limit truncation notice.

Knorvia-authored provenance similarity tooling. Syntax skeleton lines no longer count toward the comparison on either side. A line consisting only of keywords and punctuation, with at most one conventional catch binding, is the shape every implementation with error handling produces; two files sharing such a line is not evidence that one was copied from the other, and counting them only dilutes the ratio so that genuinely identical implementation lines appear to occupy a smaller share. Excluded forms are a bare try, a catch with no binding or one plain identifier, finally, else, a bare return, a lone closing brace, and an empty pair of braces. A catch carrying an additional condition clause stays in, because that clause is a written decision rather than skeleton, and so does any return that carries a value. The threshold is unchanged at zero point two: this corrects what the ratio is computed over, not what counts as passing. Both sides share the filter because candidate and comparison text go through the same normalization, and a file left with too few comparable lines is reported as such rather than dividing by zero.

Knorvia-authored provenance similarity tooling. The old-revision documentation now describes the three modes the code actually implements: omitting the old file resolves comparisons automatically against the plan baseline, passing an old file without a revision reads the working tree, and passing both uses the named revision. The earlier wording claimed a default that applied only to the first case, which let a measurement compare a candidate against its own working tree copy and report one point zero. That failure mode is now blocked: when the old file comes from the working tree and resolves to the same path and content as the candidate, the run stops and explains that such a comparison necessarily reports one point zero, so it indicates a mismatched subject rather than an unchanged file, naming both ways to obtain a real comparison. The exit is keyed on path and content together rather than on path alone, since the two layers carry absolute and relative paths respectively and those cannot be compared directly. Verified with seventy-two tests covering the guard, the explicit-revision path that must not be blocked, and the syntax-skeleton rules merged alongside.

Appending matters because entering replaces the message list rather than adding to it, which the probe confirmed by showing that a replacement list of one message yields one message regardless of how many arrived. The injected message carries an identifier, the user role, text content and a user source, all of which the message type requires. Allow and approval verdicts delegate, because submitting a prompt has no notion of permission or approval; only accept, reject and rewrite apply. Documentation gains the fact that the post-tool mount covers both the success and failure events because the runtime routes thrown tools through the same waterfall, so seven hook events need six mount points, and it gains a registered difference explaining that a post-tool denial is observable to the user because the runtime has no accept-with-warning branch and blocking rewrites the result as a failure.

Knorvia-authored hooks plugin implementation, third mount point, plus three mapping details the contract needed. The post-tool mount covers both the success and failure hook events because the runtime routes thrown tools through the same waterfall, and the result is deep-frozen so the plugin replaces outcomes by returning a decision rather than mutating the result. Three details are now written into the behaviour contract because they are semantic boundaries rather than platform gaps: an approval request answered with another request must delegate instead of claiming, since claiming would either loop or consume the user opportunity without asking anyone; a post-tool denial can only be expressed as blocking, because the tool has already run and there is nothing left to cancel, which makes it observably different from a pre-tool denial; and a post-tool approval request has no object and therefore always delegates. Each of the three has a contract test.

Knorvia-authored M2 access-package contract for the hooks plugin. This revision records the verification evidence behind the reuse claims: every contract type the plugin intends to reuse was confirmed to already exist in the contracts package, so the plugin adds no new type definitions there, and every DSH package it depends on was confirmed to be already declared by the bootstrap package, so implementation needs no new dependencies. It also records which dispatch mode each of the seven extension points uses, since the mode is what decides whether a hook can block: waterfall points can decline to delegate, the serial point short-circuits on the first bail value, and the emit point accepts only a synchronous throw as a veto, which is why an asynchronous hook cannot prevent a session from being created.

Knorvia-authored M2 access-package contract for the hooks plugin. It records which cordis extension points carry the seven hook events on the DSH runtime, together with the dispatch mode of each and what that mode permits: three points are waterfalls that can block or rewrite, one is a serial point whose first bail value short-circuits, and one is an emit point that can only veto through a synchronous throw. It also records a deviation from the plan document, where the post-tool event was assigned to a point that turns out to be observe-only, and states that the waterfall point is used instead while the observe-only one is kept for audit. Behaviour paragraphs reuse the existing core-hooks contract by reference rather than restating it, because that package is deleted at kernel switch and only its contract survives. Differences forced by the platform are registered separately with their cause, their observable effect, and whether an equivalent exists.

Knorvia-authored hooks plugin implementation, first mount point. The verdict module turns a hook permission decision into one of four outcomes and keeps the no-opinion case distinct from an explicit allow, because delegating to the next listener and asserting permission are different statements. A hook that supplies no decision is treated as having no opinion rather than as failing, since hook output is user script and a malformed result means that hook expressed nothing, not that the plugin is misconfigured. The pre-tool mount point maps those outcomes onto the tool runtime decision shape and delegates when there is no opinion, which is the common path. It carries the abort signal through unchanged because the runtime rechecks cancellation after asynchronous listeners settle, and it does not read or modify permission mode state, which belongs to the policy package. Verified with ten contract tests driving a real cordis context through the tool pre-execute waterfall, covering delegation, denial with a reason, approval requests, explicit allowance, input field mapping, short-circuiting, non-short-circuiting delegation, and listener disposal.

Knorvia-authored hooks plugin implementation, second mount point. The permission request mount maps hook verdicts onto the four approval outcomes the runtime defines. An allow becomes a one-time allowance because the runtime has no permanent-allow outcome, a deny becomes rejection, and a request for approval delegates rather than claiming the request: this event is itself the request for approval, so answering it with another request would either loop or consume the user opportunity without asking anyone. Absence of a verdict also delegates, preserving the chance for a downstream answerer to decide. The handler passes the abort signal through unchanged and tolerates every optional field being absent, since the runtime declares them optional. Verified with eight contract tests driving a real cordis context through the approval waterfall, covering all four outcomes, field mapping, absent optional fields, claiming without delegating, and listener disposal.

Knorvia-authored hooks plugin implementation, fifth mount point. The stop mount treats a denial as a request to continue, because at the point where the turn is about to close, refusing to close and asking to continue are the same statement; it expresses that by steering a user message, which the runtime reads as fresh input that runs another step. Allowance, approval requests and no opinion all leave the turn to close, since none of them has a meaning at that boundary. The handler deliberately returns no bail value so that other listeners registered at the same point still run, which keeps the aggregation equivalent to the old behaviour even though the runtime visits every listener instead of short-circuiting on the first objection; that difference is already registered. Verified with nine contract tests driving a real cordis context through the serial dispatch, covering continuation, quiet closure for each non-denial verdict, field mapping, the multi-listener aggregation, the absence of a bail value, disposal, and the injected message shape.

Knorvia-authored hooks plugin implementation, sixth mount point, which is observation only. The tool-result event carries no decision, so this module records tool name, call identity, failure flag, content block count and failure message, and produces nothing. It wraps the observer call in its own guard because the event bus does not contain listener exceptions: the runtime documentation promises containment, but that promise belongs to the runtime, not to the bus, which was measured by throwing from a listener and seeing the error reach the caller. Since observation failing must never affect tool execution, the module absorbs those errors itself rather than relying on a guarantee that does not hold at this layer. It also leaves its inputs untouched. Verified with seven contract tests covering success and failure field mapping, swallowed observer errors, multiple listeners, absent optional fields, disposal, and input immutability.
